planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped specimens in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give it room to widen slightly with age even though the habit stays strongly upright.

directions: Irish Yew is a strictly upright, spindle-shaped sport of English yew first found on a hillside in County Fermanagh, Ireland, around 1780, and every plant in cultivation today traces back to cuttings of that original find since seedlings revert to the broader, spreading species form. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, where it holds the same dense, dark, glossy needle coverage that makes true yews so valuable for deep-shade sites unsuited to most other conifers. Its narrow, multi-stemmed columns need almost no corrective pruning to keep their shape, though it accepts shearing well for a tighter formal accent or sentinel planting at entries and corners. As with all yews, every part except the fleshy red aril contains toxic taxine alkaloids and should be kept away from children, pets, and livestock.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Japanese yew is markedly more cold hardy than English yew, tolerating winters well into USDA zone 4.

directions: Japanese Yew is a broad, columnar to multi-stemmed evergreen native to Korea, China, Russia, and Japan, grown for the same dense, dark, flattened needles and fine texture prized in English yew but with much greater cold hardiness, making it a mainstay of foundation plantings and hedges across the colder half of the United States. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it thrives with little competition from other conifers, though it also tolerates considerable sun in cooler climates. It withstands heavy, repeated shearing better than almost any other woody plant, which is why it has long been a staple of formal hedges and topiary, but it also makes a handsome, informal specimen if left to develop naturally. Female plants produce small, bright red arils in fall that are the only non-toxic part of the plant; the needles, bark, and seed within the aril contain taxine alkaloids poisonous to people and livestock.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Densiformis is a low, wide-spreading female selection valued for filling foundation beds and low hedges without the height of upright yews.

directions: Densiformis is a compact, mounding hybrid yew that spreads wider than it grows tall, forming a dense, semi-dwarf mass of lustrous, dark green, thin needles well suited to low foundation plantings, informal borders, and low hedging where an upright yew would quickly outgrow the space. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, though like other Taxus x media hybrids it also tolerates considerable sun in cooler regions. As a female clone it sets small red arils in fall if a male yew is nearby for pollination, adding light winter interest, but the seed and all other plant parts remain toxic if eaten. It shears well for a tighter formal look but generally needs only light shaping to keep its naturally dense, rounded form.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring or early fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade, sheltered from winter sun and wind; this is the most cold-hardy and shade-tolerant of all yews, native to cool northeastern forests.

directions: Canadian Yew is a low, open, sprawling native shrub of cool, moist forest understories from the Canadian Maritimes and Great Lakes south into the Appalachians, spreading by irregular, ascending branches clothed in flat, dark green needles with pale undersides. It is exceptionally shade tolerant, thriving in full woodland shade where it forms loose colonies as an understory groundcover, but it needs protection from harsh winter sun and drying wind, which can scorch its foliage. Female plants bear small, bright red, fleshy arils in fall that are the only non-toxic part of the plant; the needles, bark, and seed are rich in taxine alkaloids that are highly toxic to people and livestock, though deer browse the foliage readily, often limiting the species in the wild. It requires consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil and struggles in heat, drought, or compacted ground, making it best suited to naturalized woodland gardens in cold climates.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Carolina Sapphire grows quickly and is widely used as a living Christmas tree and fast privacy screen in the Southeast.

directions: Carolina Sapphire is a fast-growing selection of Arizona cypress discovered as a chance seedling in North Carolina, prized for electric silvery-blue, feathery foliage that releases a lemony scent when crushed and for a growth rate that can exceed a foot per year under good conditions. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil, since like the species it resents standing water and heavy, poorly drained clay, which invite root and canker disease. Once established it tolerates heat and drought well and needs little supplemental irrigation, making it popular for quick screens, windbreaks, and as a cut or living Christmas tree in the Southeast. Light shaping when young encourages dense, well-furnished growth, though it generally holds a tidy pyramidal form with minimal pruning.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Plant seedlings or container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Mexican cypress comes from Central American highland cloud forests and prefers more consistent moisture than the desert cypresses of the Southwest.

directions: Mexican cypress, also called Cedar of Goa from its long cultivation history in Portuguese colonial gardens, is a fast-growing conical conifer native to the mountain forests of Mexico and Central America, with aromatic, blue-green to gray-green, finely textured foliage on a densely branched crown. Plant in moist but well-drained soil in full sun, giving supplemental water through dry spells since it comes from higher-rainfall montane habitats than the desert-adapted Arizona and Italian cypresses. It grows rapidly, often a foot or more per year when young, making it a popular choice for quick screens, windbreaks, and reforestation plantings in warm climates, though it needs staking or wind protection while establishing its root system. It has little tolerance for hard freezes and is best reserved for USDA zone 8 and warmer.
scientific_name_note: Some current taxonomic treatments place this species in the genus Hesperocyparis as Hesperocyparis lusitanica, though Cupressus lusitanica remains in wide horticultural use.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant seedlings or container-grown trees in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Bhutan cypress is a large, fast-growing Himalayan conifer best suited to mild-winter regions in zone 8 and warmer.

directions: Bhutan cypress is a large, graceful conifer native to limestone slopes of the western Himalaya, where it is planted around temples and monasteries and valued for aromatic, durable timber; in cultivation it forms a broadly pyramidal tree with drooping branchlets of dark green, scale-like foliage. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, with regular water during establishment, since it grows naturally in seasonally moist montane forest rather than true desert conditions. It grows at a moderate to fast pace once established and develops into a substantial specimen or windbreak tree, so it needs considerable open space away from structures and power lines. It has only moderate cold tolerance and is best grown in USDA zone 8 and warmer, where it is largely untroubled by pests or disease.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; give this weeping South African tree ample overhead and side room to display its long, drooping foliage.

directions: Long-Leaved Yellowwood is a graceful South African forest tree prized for its distinctly weeping habit and unusually long, narrow, drooping needle-like leaves that set it apart from the stiffer, shorter foliage of most other podocarps. Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; as a forest-margin species in its native range it tolerates significant shade, especially when young, and appreciates protection from the hottest afternoon sun in inland climates. It is slow to moderate in growth and eventually forms a substantial, elegant specimen or screening tree, making it a favored choice for parks and large gardens in frost-free regions. It has little tolerance for hard freezes and performs best in USDA zone 9 and warmer with consistent moisture.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Alpine Totara is the most cold-hardy podocarp in general cultivation and spreads into a low, wide mat useful as an evergreen groundcover.

directions: Alpine Totara is a low, sprawling New Zealand alpine conifer with dense, leathery, olive-green needles on wide-spreading branches that root as they creep, gradually forming a thick evergreen mat useful in rock gardens, mixed shrub borders, and as a durable groundcover. Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; it takes more sun in cool coastal climates but benefits from afternoon shade where summers are hot. It is the hardiest species in the genus Podocarpus, tolerating colder winters than the tree-form podocarps commonly grown in the Gulf South, which makes it a useful shade-tolerant evergreen option further north. Growth is slow to moderate, and established plants need only occasional watering, tolerating short dry spells once their roots are established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; this Chilean species has an elegant weeping habit and appreciates a sheltered site out of drying wind.

directions: Willow-Leaf Podocarpus is a graceful, arching Chilean conifer named for its long, narrow, soft, willow-like leaves, quite unlike the shorter, stiffer foliage of most other podocarps, and it has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its ornamental value. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; in its native temperate rainforest habitat it grows under a fairly humid, moderate climate, so it performs best with consistent moisture and appreciates some shelter from harsh midday sun and drying wind. Female plants bear small, fleshy, reddish fruit when a male is grown nearby for pollination, adding modest ornamental interest. It is moderately cold hardy for the genus but still best reserved for USDA zone 8 and warmer, where its slow, weeping growth makes an outstanding specimen or accent tree.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Upright Plum Yew (Columnar Japanese Plum Yew)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; full sun in hot climates can cause winter foliage burn, while full shade encourages the habit to loosen and splay.

directions: Upright Plum Yew is a distinctive, slow-growing, strongly columnar selection of Japanese plum yew, with dark green needles held in a striking bottlebrush arrangement around upright stems that stay narrow and dense for a decade or more before slowly broadening with age. Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial shade, since it holds its tight columnar form best out of the hottest afternoon sun, though deep shade tends to cause the habit to open up and lose density. Like the species, it tolerates root competition, heat, and humidity far better than true yews and is not browsed by deer, making it a dependable vertical accent for shaded foundation plantings, narrow side yards, or formal entry plantings. It is low-maintenance and slow-growing, requiring little pruning beyond removing the occasional wayward shoot.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Prostrate Plum Yew (Spreading Japanese Plum Yew)

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; this low, mounding selection makes an excellent evergreen groundcover beneath trees where turf and most other groundcovers struggle.

directions: Prostrate Plum Yew is a low, spreading selection of Japanese plum yew with the same dense, dark, glossy, yew-like needles as the species but a sprawling, mounding habit that stays well under three feet tall while spreading considerably wider, making it a valuable evergreen groundcover for shaded woodland gardens. Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in partial to full shade, where it tolerates the deep shade and root competition of mature trees far better than turf grass or most flowering groundcovers. It is not browsed by deer, unlike Taxus yews, which makes it especially useful in landscapes with heavy deer pressure. Slow-growing and low-maintenance, it needs virtually no pruning to maintain its naturally graceful, spreading form and tolerates both moist and moderately dry shaded soils once established.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade in spring or fall; give it more room than Japanese plum yew, since it grows into a larger, looser shrub or small tree.

directions: Chinese Plum Yew bears the longest, darkest needles of any commonly cultivated Cephalotaxus, with a soft, drooping texture and conspicuous white stomatal bands on the undersides, giving it a lusher, more dramatic look than the more compact Japanese plum yew. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, where it develops into a large, loose, multi-stemmed shrub or small tree over time; it also tolerates considerable heat and shade, though it appreciates more consistent moisture than its Japanese relative. Like other plum yews it is not browsed by deer and produces fleshy, olive-colored, plum-like fruit on female plants that is alkaloid-free, unlike the toxic seed of true Taxus yews. It is slow-growing and long-lived, making an excellent large screening or specimen shrub for shaded woodland gardens in zones 7 to 9.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; California Nutmeg is a slow-growing understory conifer of California's coastal and Sierra Nevada forests that tolerates deep woodland shade far better than most conifers.

directions: California Nutmeg is the largest species of Torreya, a slow-growing, sharply needled evergreen native to shaded canyons and forest understories of the California Coast Ranges and Sierra Nevada, where it can persist for decades beneath a closed forest canopy. Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; it tolerates significant shade even as a mature tree, though growth is slower in deep shade than in filtered light, and it appreciates consistent soil moisture and cool root conditions. Its stiff, glossy, dark green needles end in a sharp point, unlike the softer foliage of true yews, and female trees produce a large, plum-like fruit enclosing a single seed that resembles a true nutmeg, though it is unrelated to the tropical spice tree. It is a long-lived, low-maintenance woodland tree well suited to naturalized shade gardens within its native and near-native range.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Japanese Torreya is a slow-growing understory conifer traditionally valued in Japan both for its edible seed and its fine, close-grained wood.

directions: Japanese Torreya, known as Kaya in Japan, is a slow-growing, shade-tolerant conifer with stiff, glossy, dark green needles ending in a sharp point, long cultivated for its plum-like fruit enclosing an edible seed that is roasted and eaten or pressed for a fragrant cooking oil. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it grows naturally as a forest understory tree and tolerates far less light than most conifers grown in American gardens. Its fine-grained, aromatic, pale yellow wood is prized in Japan above nearly all other timber for crafting go boards (goban), valued for its resilience, subtle fragrance, and the satisfying sound it produces when stones are placed on it. Growth is slow and the tree is long-lived, making it best suited to patient gardeners with a shaded, sheltered site and consistently moist soil.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
